units.title: International Political Economy
units.description: This unit explores the intersection of politics and economics on a global scale, focusing on trade, international finance, development, and the impact of globalization.

lectures.title: Trade
lectures.description: This lecture examines the underlying logic of international trade, the political battles over market access, and the institutional frameworks that manage global commerce.

sessions.title: Comparative Advantage
sessions.description: In this session, you will learn the core economic theory of comparative advantage, which explains why states benefit from specialization even if one state is more efficient at producing everything. By the end of this session, you will be able to calculate simple trade gains and explain why isolationism is mathematically costly. Understanding this logic is essential for moving past the intuition of trade as a 'zero-sum' competition to a 'positive-sum' framework.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the intuitive, zero-sum view of trade. Most students instinctively view international trade through a 'winner and loser' lens, often assuming that if a country is more productive in every industry (Absolute Advantage), it has no reason to trade with others. To break this misconception, use a whiteboard to illustrate a world with two countries and two products—for example, Wheat and Computers. The core mission here is to move the learner from thinking about 'who is faster' to 'what is being sacrificed' by producing one good over another.

Introduce the central mechanism: Opportunity Cost. On the board, draw a simple productivity matrix. Define opportunity cost not just as a financial price, but as the amount of one good a country must give up to produce one unit of another good. This is the 'unlock' moment: by showing that even a highly efficient country cannot be in two places at once, you demonstrate that time and resources spent on one product are inherently taken away from another. Explain that Comparative Advantage is found where the opportunity cost is lowest. It is vital to emphasize that while a country might have an absolute advantage in both goods, it is mathematically impossible for it to have a comparative advantage in both.

Transition into a live calculation exercise. Ask the learners to determine which country should specialize in which product based on a specific ratio of production. This practice isn't just about the math; it’s designed to reveal the 'specialization gap.' When learners see that the total global output increases when countries focus on their lowest-opportunity-cost goods, the 'positive-sum' nature of trade becomes visible. If a student struggles, address the 'efficiency trap'—the idea that it feels 'wrong' to import something you are good at making. Clarify that by importing what you are merely 'good' at, you free up resources to produce what you are 'best' at.

Conclude by tying these mathematical gains to the geopolitical cost of isolationism. Use the whiteboard to show that a state attempting to produce everything domestically (Autarky) essentially forces its citizens to pay the highest possible 'opportunity cost' for every item. This sets the stage for the rest of the unit: if trade is mathematically beneficial for the aggregate, why do we see so much political resistance to it? This question bridges the gap between pure economic theory and the domestic political battles discussed in the next session.

tasks: Identify the opportunity cost for two hypothetical countries producing two different goods.
Determine which country should specialize in which product based on the principle of comparative advantage.

sessions.title: The Politics of Trade
sessions.description: This session explores the domestic winners and losers of trade using the Stolper-Samuelson and Ricardo-Viner models to explain why certain groups lobby for or against open markets. You will gain the ability to predict which industries or labor groups will oppose trade agreements in a given political economy. This bridges the gap between abstract economic theory and the messy political reality of why states don't always choose the 'optimal' economic path.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by pivoting from the previous session's ideal of 'Comparative Advantage'—where trade is a rising tide lifting all boats—to the friction of domestic reality. The core puzzle we must solve is this: if trade creates aggregate wealth for a nation, why is it so politically toxic? This session transitions the student from thinking of the state as a single rational actor to a 'black box' filled with competing domestic interests. I start by visualizing a national economy not as a single entity, but as a collection of 'factors' (Land, Labor, and Capital) and 'sectors' (specific industries like Agriculture or Tech). The primary goal is to demonstrate that while trade makes the 'pie' larger, the slicing of that pie creates profound losers who have every incentive to block the process.

To unpack the first major theoretical lens, we introduce the Stolper-Samuelson Theorem. This model assumes 'factor mobility,' meaning a worker can easily move from a declining shoe factory to a booming software firm. In this world, trade preferences are split along class lines. If a country like the US is capital-abundant but labor-scarce, trade benefits owners of capital and hurts workers. I will explain the logic: trade increases the demand for what a country is 'good' at producing (capital-intensive goods), driving up returns for those who own that factor, while the influx of cheap labor-intensive imports drives down wages. The key insight for the student is that in this model, a billionaire and a venture capitalist find common ground against a unified labor front, regardless of the industry they are in. I’ll warn students of the common misconception that this is about 'rich vs. poor'; it is specifically about which resource you provide to the economy.

Next, we contrast this with the Ricardo-Viner (or Specific Factors) model, which is much more realistic for the short-to-medium term. Here, factors are 'stuck' in their industries—a steel worker cannot simply become a web developer overnight. In this visualization, the conflict isn't between Labor and Capital, but between different sectors. I will describe how the owner of a steel mill and the workers in that mill suddenly find themselves on the same side, lobbying for protection against foreign steel, while the export-oriented tech sector lobbies for more open trade. This creates a more fragmented political map. The crucial distinction to emphasize is 'Factor Mobility': if it's high, we see class warfare (Stolper-Samuelson); if it's low, we see industry-vs-industry warfare (Ricardo-Viner).

To ground these theories, we conduct a mental simulation of a historical trade agreement, such as NAFTA or a contemporary regional pact. I will ask the students to predict who would show up to protest at the statehouse. If we see a coalition of various labor unions from different industries, they are behaving according to Stolper-Samuelson logic. If we see a specific industry group—both CEOs and union reps—petitioning for a targeted tariff, they are operating in the Ricardo-Viner world. This exercise reveals whether students can identify 'Factor Mobility' in the real world and explains why modern trade politics often feels like a messy patchwork of special interest groups rather than a clean ideological divide.

Finally, we address the 'Collective Action Problem' of trade politics. Even if the winners (consumers) outnumber the losers (specific workers), the losers are 'concentrated' while the winners are 'diffuse.' I will explain that a worker losing their livelihood has a massive incentive to lobby, whereas a consumer saving $5 a year on cheaper shirts has almost no incentive to go to Washington. This explains the 'protectionist bias' in democracy. We conclude by framing this as the 'bottleneck' of global commerce: economic efficiency is often sacrificed at the altar of domestic political survival. This sets the stage for the next session on the specific tools—like tariffs and quotas—that politicians use to appease these vocal domestic losers.

tasks: Compare the Stolper-Samuelson model with the Ricardo-Viner model regarding factor mobility.
Analyze a historical trade agreement and identify which domestic interest groups likely supported or opposed it.

sessions.title: Protectionism
sessions.description: You will learn about the various tools of protectionism—including tariffs, quotas, and non-tariff barriers—and the 'infant industry' argument for their use. This session enables you to evaluate the strategic and political motivations for trade wars and domestic subsidies. This is critical for understanding the current global shift toward industrial policy and the return of economic nationalism.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start this session by acknowledging the tension between the theoretical ideal of free trade discussed in previous sessions and the messy political reality of why states actively block market access. The central objective is to transition from the 'how-to' of trade to the 'how-to-prevent' it, framing protectionism not just as an economic error, but as a deliberate strategic tool. Begin the visual conceptual mapping by drawing a wall between two trading blocks, labeling it 'The Barrier.' This serves as the anchor for defining protectionism: the use of state power to shield domestic producers from foreign competition. Emphasize that while free trade maximizes global efficiency, protectionism prioritizes domestic stability, security, or specific interest groups, setting the stage for the 'why' behind trade wars.

Moving into the mechanics, introduce the 'Tax and Limit' framework to categorize protectionist tools. Start with Tariffs—the most visible tool—explained as a tax on imports that artificially raises prices to help local firms compete. Contrast this with Quotas, which are physical limits on quantity. Most importantly, spend time on 'Non-Tariff Barriers' (NTBs). Educators should visualize these as 'invisible hurdles,' such as complex health and safety regulations, local content requirements, or burdensome administrative procedures. A key teaching point here is that as formal tariffs have dropped due to international treaties, NTBs have proliferated because they are harder to detect and easier to justify as 'public safety' rather than 'trade manipulation.' This prevents the common misconception that trade is becoming 'freer' simply because tariff rates are low.

Shift the focus to the 'Infant Industry' argument, which serves as the intellectual backbone for many protectionist policies. Use the metaphor of a nursery: a young industry (like renewable energy or high-tech semiconductors in a developing nation) cannot compete with established global giants immediately. It needs a 'protective greenhouse' to grow until it achieves economies of scale. However, immediately introduce the 'Dinosaur Trap' critique—the idea that protected industries often lose the incentive to ever become efficient because they are shielded from the very competition that drives innovation. This creates a logical bridge to understanding current industrial policies, where states are no longer just protecting 'weak' industries but are strategically subsidizing 'future' industries for national security reasons.

Conclude the session by examining the 'Economic Nationalism' feedback loop. Explain that when one state uses protectionism, it often triggers a 'tit-for-tat' response, leading to a trade war. Use a quick exercise where students must identify three non-tariff barriers a country might use to block a specific product (like foreign electric vehicles) without calling it a 'tax.' This exercise is designed to reveal if learners can see past the rhetoric of 'standards' to the underlying protectionist intent. The final synthesis should leave the teacher and student with the understanding that while protectionism is often 'bad' economics (reducing total wealth), it is frequently perceived as 'good' politics, which explains its persistence in the modern global order.

tasks: Define three different types of non-tariff barriers.
Explain the 'infant industry' argument and its common critiques in a short paragraph.

sessions.title: Trade Institutions
sessions.description: This session introduces the World Trade Organization (WTO) and the GATT system, focusing on principles like 'Most Favored Nation' status and dispute resolution. You will understand how these institutions lower transaction costs and resolve collective action problems among trading states. This session provides the formal institutional context needed to analyze the current crisis of multilateralism in the trade regime.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this final session of the Trade lecture by pivoting from the 'why' and 'who' of trade to the 'how'—specifically, the architectural framework that prevents global commerce from descending into a series of retaliatory trade wars. Following our discussion on protectionism, it is natural to ask: if every state has a domestic incentive to cheat or protect its industries, why doesn't the system collapse? The teacher should frame this as a 'Collective Action Problem.' Without a central authority, states face a Prisoner's Dilemma where mutual defection (protectionism) is the Nash equilibrium, even though mutual cooperation (free trade) is better for everyone. This sets the stage for the World Trade Organization (WTO) not as a world government, but as a commitment device designed to lower transaction costs and monitor compliance.

The first pillar of this architecture to illustrate on the whiteboard is the 'Most Favored Nation' (MFN) principle. This is the 'Golden Rule' of multilateralism: if you give one member a special trade favor, you must give the same favor to all other members. The teacher should explain that this prevents the creation of exclusive trade blocs that historically fueled geopolitical tensions. However, it is vital to clarify the common misconceptions regarding 'exceptions.' Explain that Regional Trade Agreements (like USMCA) and the 'Generalized System of Preferences' for developing nations are not 'cheating' the MFN, but are legally codified carve-outs designed to promote specific types of integration or development. This distinction is crucial because it helps students see the WTO as a flexible contract rather than a rigid, brittle set of rules.

Moving to the 'engine room' of the system, we introduce the WTO Dispute Settlement Mechanism (DSM). Use a flow-chart visualization here to show the progression from 'Consultations' to 'Panel Reports' and finally 'Appellate Body' reviews. The most important concept here is 'negative consensus'—the idea that a ruling is automatically adopted unless *everyone* (including the winner) votes against it. This effectively gives the WTO 'teeth' that other international organizations lack. To make this concrete, the teacher should walk through a hypothetical scenario where Country A hits Country B with an illegal tariff. The goal is to show that the system isn't about 'punishing' a country with a fine, but about restoring the balance of concessions, often by authorizing the victim to 'retaliate' in a controlled, legal manner.

We conclude by addressing the 'bottleneck' of the current era: the crisis of multilateralism. The teacher should explain that the DSM is currently paralyzed because the 'Appellate Body' lacks enough judges to function, often due to a lack of consensus on appointments. This creates a bridge back to the earlier sessions on politics; when the formal institution fails to resolve disputes, states return to unilateral protectionism. This final section serves as a synthesis of the entire lecture: trade is an economic blessing (Comparative Advantage), a political minefield (Stolper-Samuelson), a strategic temptation (Protectionism), and an institutional challenge (the WTO). The practice task for students—outlining the DSM steps—is not just a memory exercise; it is a diagnostic tool to see if they understand how law replaces raw power in the international system.

tasks: Explain the 'Most Favored Nation' (MFN) principle and its exceptions.
Outline the steps of the WTO's dispute settlement mechanism.

lectures.title: Money and Development
lectures.description: This lecture investigates the global financial architecture, the mechanics of international monetary systems, and the persistent challenges of economic development and inequality.

sessions.title: Monetary Systems
sessions.description: In this session, you will explore the evolution of the global monetary system from the Gold Standard to Bretton Woods and the current floating exchange rate regime. You will learn to differentiate between fixed and floating rates and the implications each has for national sovereignty and stability. This provides the foundation for understanding how global finance restricts the domestic policy choices of modern governments.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by framing money not just as a tool for trade, but as a central expression of state power and a constraint on national sovereignty. The lecture begins with a whiteboard visualization of the 'Evolution of Trust'—moving from the intrinsic value of the Gold Standard to the institutional trust of the Bretton Woods system. The goal here is to explain that every international monetary system is an attempt to solve the same problem: how to facilitate trade between nations that use different currencies while preventing chaotic swings in value. Use the metaphor of 'The Rules of the Game' to describe how the Gold Standard forced internal domestic prices to adjust to international gold flows, effectively prioritizing global stability over local employment.

Transition to the collapse of the Gold Standard and the birth of the Bretton Woods system in 1944. On the whiteboard, draw a bridge between 'Fixed Rates' and 'Flexibility.' Explain that Bretton Woods was a hybrid system: currencies were pegged to the US Dollar, which was in turn pegged to gold. This part of the lecture must highlight the importance of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) as the 'referee' of this system. The core logic to convey is that this era allowed for some domestic policy autonomy (like funding a welfare state) because capital didn't move as freely across borders as it does today. Address a common misconception here: learners often think we are still on the Gold Standard; clarify that since 1971, we have lived in a world of 'fiat' currency where value is derived from state credit and market confidence.

Introduce the 'Mundell-Fleming Trilemma' (The Impossible Trinity) as the session's conceptual peak. Visualize this as a triangle with three vertices: 1) A Fixed Exchange Rate, 2) Capital Mobility (the ability for money to move in and out of a country freely), and 3) Independent Monetary Policy (the ability for a central bank to set interest rates). Explain the hard logic that a state can only ever pick two sides of the triangle. Use a real-world scenario to make this concrete: if a country wants to keep its currency value stable (Fixed) to attract investors and let those investors move money freely (Capital Mobility), it must give up control over its interest rates. If it tries to lower interest rates to boost its own economy, money will flee to higher-interest countries, breaking the fixed exchange rate. This 'pick-two' logic is the fundamental constraint of modern globalization.

Conclude by asking the learners to map current global powers onto the Trilemma triangle. For example, explain why the United States chooses Capital Mobility and Independent Monetary Policy (letting the dollar 'float' and fluctuate) while many smaller emerging markets struggle with the trade-offs of fixing their currency to the dollar. This final synthesis should leave the learner with the realization that a country’s choice in the monetary system is a political statement about whether they value international stability or domestic control more. Use a quick check-in task asking them to explain why a country can't 'have it all,' which reveals if they have grasped the internal contradiction of the Trilemma before moving into the specifics of financial crises in the next session.

tasks: Contrast the Gold Standard with the Bretton Woods system.
Explain the 'Mundell-Fleming Trilemma' (the impossible trinity) in your own words.

sessions.title: Financial Crises
sessions.description: This session examines the causes and consequences of global financial crises, focusing on capital flight, contagion, and the role of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) as a lender of last resort. You will be able to trace how a crisis in one emerging market can trigger a global downturn through financial interconnectedness. This is vital for analyzing the trade-offs between financial stability and political autonomy.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by visualizing the global financial system not as a series of isolated bank accounts, but as a high-pressure plumbing network. Explain that while session 1 focused on the 'valves' (exchange rates), this session is about what happens when the pipes burst. Introduce the concept of a Financial Crisis by emphasizing the psychological shift from confidence to panic. The core logic to convey is that finance relies on the belief that assets have value; once that belief evaporates, a rational individual response (selling assets) leads to a collective catastrophe (market collapse).

Transition to the concept of 'Capital Flight' by describing a hypothetical investor who sees trouble brewing in an emerging market. Use a whiteboard mapping to show the 'Exit' logic: when investors fear devaluation or default, they rush to convert local currency into dollars and move it abroad. This isn't just a loss of money; it’s a sudden drain of the country's foreign reserves, which we established as crucial in the previous session. Explain that this creates a feedback loop: the flight causes the currency to crash, which makes the remaining debt harder to pay, which triggers more flight. This visualization helps learners see why crises are often 'self-fulfilling prophecies' rather than just the result of bad math.

Introduce 'Contagion' as the mechanism of international relations. Explain how a crisis in Thailand in 1997 could end up hurting Russia or Brazil. Use the metaphor of 'Portfolio Rebalancing'—when a fund loses money in one place, they sell off assets in unrelated 'healthy' places to cover their losses. This clarifies for the learner that financial interconnectedness is a double-edged sword: it provides capital during the good times but acts as a viral vector during the bad. A common misconception is that crises only happen to 'bad' economies; emphasize that contagion can take down relatively stable systems through sheer proximity or shared investor profiles.

Now, introduce the International Monetary Fund (IMF) as the 'Global Fire Department' or 'Lender of Last Resort.' Explain that their role is to provide the liquidity that private markets refuse to give during a panic. However, this help isn't free. This is the moment to dive into 'Conditionalities.' Frame these not just as a list of rules, but as a political trade-off: the IMF provides the cash to stop the bleeding, but in exchange, the state must undergo 'Structural Adjustment' (e.g., cutting spending, raising interest rates). Ask the students to consider why this is controversial—it often forces a government to choose between satisfying the IMF and providing for its own citizens, highlighting the tension between global stability and national sovereignty.

Conclude by setting up a comparative exercise between the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis and the 2008 Global Financial Crisis. The goal is for learners to see that while the triggers differ (currency pegs vs. subprime mortgages), the underlying anatomy—excessive leverage, sudden loss of confidence, and the desperate need for a lender of last resort—remains constant. Use this to reinforce the 'Concept-First' approach: once they understand the mechanics of a run on the bank, they can analyze any crisis in history. This leads naturally into the next session's focus on how these financial shocks dictate the long-term development paths of nations.

tasks: Identify the primary triggers of the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis or the 2008 Global Financial Crisis.
List two common 'conditionalities' the IMF might impose on a country receiving a loan.

sessions.title: Development and Aid
sessions.description: You will learn about the different strategies for economic development, including Import Substitution Industrialization (ISI) versus Export-Oriented Industrialization (EOI). This session helps you understand why some nations escaped the poverty trap while others remained stagnant despite foreign aid. This addresses the 'Mastery' goal of comparing policy effectiveness across different historical and regional contexts.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by posing a fundamental puzzle: why did two regions, Latin America and East Asia, which started with similar economic profiles in the 1950s, diverge so dramatically by the 1990s? This session moves from the previous discussion on financial crises to the long-term structural strategies states use to grow their way out of poverty. Use the whiteboard to draw a simple 'Dependency Loop'—the idea that developing nations were stuck producing raw materials while buying expensive finished goods from the North. This sets the stage for the first major strategy: Import Substitution Industrialization (ISI). Explain that ISI was born out of a desire for autonomy; by building domestic industries behind high tariff walls, countries like Brazil and Argentina tried to 'break the loop.' The key takeaway here is the logic of self-sufficiency versus the reality of creating inefficient, protected industries that eventually lacked the competitive pressure to innovate.

Contrast this on the other side of the board with the Export-Oriented Industrialization (EOI) model adopted by the 'Four Asian Tigers' (South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore). Explain the logical pivot: instead of shunning the global market, these states embraced it, but with heavy state guidance. Illustrate a 'Product Cycle' on the board, showing how these nations started with low-tech textiles and moved up the value chain to electronics. The crucial distinction to emphasize is that while ISI focuses on the 'Home' market, EOI uses the 'Global' market as a disciplining mechanism. A common misconception for students is that EOI is 'pure free market' capitalism; clarify that it actually involved significant state intervention, subsidies, and strategic planning, just directed outward rather than inward.

Transition to the role of foreign aid as a lubricant or a trap for these development engines. Introduce the 'Aid Paradox': why does more money sometimes lead to less growth? Explain the logic of 'Dutch Disease' or the 'Resource Curse' of aid, where an influx of foreign cash can devalue the local manufacturing sector and foster corruption or 'rent-seeking' behavior. Use a hypothetical scenario where a government receives a massive grant—ask the students to consider whether that money goes toward a long-term dam project (infrastructure) or short-term subsidies to keep the public happy. This practice moment is designed to reveal whether students understand the political-economic trade-offs between immediate stability and long-term investment.

Conclude the session by synthesizing these paths into the 'Poverty Trap' concept. Explain that development is not just about the volume of capital, but the institutional 'plumbing' that directs it. For the final whiteboard mapping, connect the internal policy choice (ISI vs. EOI) with external assistance (Aid). The goal is for the learner to see that development is a 'bottleneck' problem: if a state has the wrong strategy (ISI in a globalized world) or the wrong institutions, more money—whether through loans or aid—will only exacerbate the underlying debt or dependency issues. This prepares them for the final session on global inequality by showing that 'success' is a mix of strategic policy and favorable global conditions.

tasks: Compare the development trajectories of Latin America (ISI) and East Asia (EOI).
Evaluate the pros and cons of foreign aid in promoting long-term growth.

sessions.title: Global Inequality
sessions.description: This session analyzes the structural causes of inequality between the 'Global North' and 'Global South,' looking at historical legacies and modern institutional biases. You will gain a nuanced perspective on why the gap between rich and poor states persists despite increasing global wealth. This session synthesizes the lecture by connecting monetary policy and development strategy to the broader issue of justice in the international system.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by drawing a stark horizontal line across the whiteboard, labeling the top half 'Global North' and the bottom 'Global South.' Use this visual to transition from the technical mechanics of money and trade discussed earlier to the ethical and structural reality of the international system: the persistent wealth gap. The goal here is to shift the learner's focus from 'how' the economy works to 'why' it seems to work better for some than for others. Introduce the concept of structural inequality as a 'sticky' problem that persists despite the theoretical predictions of neoclassical economics, which suggest that capital should flow to where it is scarce and generate growth.

Introduce Dependency Theory by illustrating a 'Core-Periphery' map on the board. Instead of states being independent actors, draw arrows showing raw materials flowing from the periphery to the core, and high-value manufactured goods flowing back. Explain that the primary insight here is that the 'underdevelopment' of the South is not a natural starting phase that every country goes through, but an active product of how the global economy is structured. Address the common misconception that poor countries are simply 'behind' on a linear path of progress; clarify that for dependency theorists, the global market is a rigged game where the rules favor the owners of capital and technology, effectively trapping the South in a role of low-value production.

Transition to the role of modern institutions by discussing Intellectual Property (IP) laws as a contemporary 'gatekeeper.' On the whiteboard, draw a circle representing a new life-saving drug or a sustainable energy technology. Explain how TRIPs (Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights) under the WTO can create a paradox: while they incentivize innovation in the North, they often price out the South from the very tools needed for development or public health. Use this to prompt a reflection on the 'Developmental Bottleneck'—how can a state industrialize if the ladder of imitation (which the North used in the 19th century) has been pulled up through modern legal regimes? This connects the session back to the EOI/ISI strategies from the previous session, showing how global rules now constrain those domestic choices.

Conclude the session with a synthesis exercise that asks the learner to weigh 'Internal' vs. 'External' causes of inequality. Ask them to identify two specific ways IP laws impact a developing nation's budget. This isn't just a recall task; it’s designed to reveal whether the learner understands the trade-off between participating in the global rules-based order and the cost of that participation for a poor state. Finish by framing the entire unit’s progression: from the 'Impossible Trinity' of monetary policy to the 'Structural Trap' of inequality, reinforcing that in International Relations, economic choices are always deeply political and moral choices.

tasks: Define the 'Dependency Theory' perspective on global inequality.
Identify two ways in which current international intellectual property laws may affect development in poor countries.

lectures.title: Globalization
lectures.description: This lecture synthesizes the trade and financial concepts to analyze the current era of hyper-globalization, its corporate drivers, and the political backlash it has inspired.

sessions.title: Multinational Firms
sessions.description: You will learn about the role of Multinational Corporations (MNCs) as key non-state actors and how they navigate or manipulate national jurisdictions through Foreign Direct Investment (FDI). This session enables you to evaluate the power dynamics between global firms and sovereign states. Understanding MNCs is crucial for seeing how economic power is often decentralized away from government capitals.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by challenging the Westphalian assumption that states are the only relevant actors in international relations. Use the whiteboard to draw a simple map of global power where capitals like Washington or Beijing are traditional hubs, but then introduce 'corporate islands'—Multinational Corporations (MNCs)—that exist across borders. Explain that an MNC isn't just a big company that exports; it is a firm that owns and controls production facilities in more than one country. This distinction is vital because it moves us from 'trade' (buying and selling across borders) to 'investment' (owning the means of production inside another sovereign's territory). 

Introduce Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) as the primary tool of these firms. On the board, contrast 'Horizontal FDI' with 'Vertical FDI' using a relatable industry like automotive or tech. Describe Horizontal FDI as 'duplication': a company building a factory in Europe to serve the European market, primarily to avoid tariffs or transportation costs. Then, contrast this with Vertical FDI, which is 'fragmentation': slicing the production process and placing different stages in different countries to exploit specific local advantages, such as low-cost labor in Vietnam or high-tech engineering in Germany. This conceptual move helps learners see that the global economy isn't a series of independent markets, but a deeply integrated web managed by private boardrooms.

Transition into the power struggle between these firms and sovereign states. The central tension is the 'Obsolescing Bargain' vs. the 'Race to the Bottom.' Explain that while states want the capital, jobs, and technology that MNCs bring, MNCs want profit maximization and low regulatory hurdles. Use the 'Race to the Bottom' logic to show how MNCs can play governments against one another. If Country A raises corporate taxes or environmental standards, the MNC threatens to move to Country B. This creates a scenario where sovereign states actually lose the ability to regulate their own internal affairs because they are terrified of 'capital flight.' Visualizing this as a competitive auction where states are the bidders and corporations are the prize helps clarify why small or developing nations often feel their sovereignty is eroded.

Address a common misconception: that MNCs are always 'predatory' or that states are 'powerless.' Use a brief practice moment to ask how a state might 'trap' an MNC once it has already built a massive, multi-billion dollar semiconductor plant. This reveals the 'Obsolescing Bargain'—once the investment is fixed in the ground, the power dynamic shifts back toward the state, which can then change the rules or increase taxes. The session should conclude by reinforcing that the modern global order is a 'dual-authority' system where political power (states) and economic power (MNCs) are in a constant, restless negotiation, fundamentally decentralizing control away from traditional government capitals.

tasks: Distinguish between horizontal and vertical Foreign Direct Investment.
Explain how MNCs use 'race to the bottom' logic to negotiate with governments.

sessions.title: Supply Chains
sessions.description: This session explains the logic of Global Value Chains (GVCs) and how the fragmentation of production has changed the nature of trade and interdependence. You will be able to analyze how a disruption in one part of the world (e.g., a pandemic or conflict) ripples through the global economy. This provides a modern lens on 'Interdependence' introduced back in Unit 2.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by sketching a single, isolated rectangle on the board to represent a traditional factory—the 20th-century model where raw materials entered one door and a finished car or radio exited the other. Contrast this with a sprawling, messy network of lines connecting multiple countries. This introduces the fundamental shift from 'Trade in Goods' to 'Trade in Tasks.' Explain that modern globalization isn't about shipping containers full of shoes; it's about Global Value Chains (GVCs), where the production process is fragmented into discrete stages, each performed where it is most efficient. This concept is the heartbeat of modern economic interdependence and challenges the old-school idea that a product has a single 'country of origin.'

Transition to the logic of 'Fragmentation.' Ask the learners to imagine an iPhone. Use the board to map a simplified version of its journey: design in California, high-end chips from Taiwan, camera modules from Japan, and assembly in China. The critical insight here is that the 'value' is added incrementally. Explain that because components cross borders multiple times before a product is finished, traditional trade statistics are often misleading. A common pitfall for students is thinking that if a product is 'Made in China,' China captured all the profit. Clarify that for a $1,000 phone, the assembly stage might only account for $10–$20 of value-added. This visualization helps learners grasp the 'Smiling Curve' concept, where the most value is at the beginning (R&D) and the end (branding/marketing), rather than the middle manufacturing stage.

Introduce the 'Fragility of Efficiency.' Now that we have mapped this complex web, simulate a disruption. Erase one node—perhaps a port strike in a specific region or a factory shutdown due to a pandemic. Draw 'ripple arrows' moving outward through the entire network. This demonstrates how GVCs transform local shocks into global crises. The key takeaway is the trade-off between 'Just-in-Time' efficiency (saving costs) and 'Just-in-Case' resilience (protecting against shocks). This leads into a discussion on why interdependence is no longer just a liberal ideal of peace through trade, but a strategic vulnerability that states must manage. We are moving from the 1990s optimism of 'infinite connection' to a realistic assessment of systemic risk.

Wrap up by discussing the 'Tariff Paradox.' Explain why traditional trade weapons, like the tariffs discussed in earlier units, are blunt and often counterproductive in the era of GVCs. If a country imposes a tariff on an 'imported' good, they are often inadvertently taxing their own domestic components that were sent abroad for assembly. Use this to explain why trade wars are so difficult to 'win' today: the lines between 'us' and 'them' are physically blurred within the product itself. Engage the learners in a thought exercise: if they were to map the supply chain of their laptop, could they even identify a single country to sanction without hurting their own economy? This exercise reveals the 'bottleneck' of modern policy: the economic reality of deep integration has outpaced the political reality of national borders.

tasks: Map the supply chain of a common consumer electronic device.
Discuss how GVCs make traditional trade wars (like tariffs) more complex to execute.

sessions.title: Backlash and Populism
sessions.description: In this session, you will examine the socio-political reaction to globalization, focusing on the rise of populist movements that argue global trade has eroded national sovereignty and identity. You will understand the link between economic displacement and political instability in Western democracies. This session prepares you to discuss the 'Future International Order' in the final unit.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by drawing a stark contrast on the board between the 'Globalist Promise' of the 1990s and the current political landscape. We must frame this not just as a policy shift, but as a crisis of legitimacy. Remind students of our previous discussions on trade efficiency; then, pivot to the 'Heckscher-Ohlin' logic to explain that while trade increases national wealth, it creates distinct winners and losers. Use a visual representation—a seesaw—to show how the gains of tech workers and financial elites in developed nations often come at the expense of manufacturing workers. This visual helps dismantle the myth that 'everyone wins' in globalization, which is a common misconception that prevents students from understanding populist anger.

Moving into the 'Backlash' phase, introduce the concept of the 'Rust Belt' effect as a universal phenomenon, not just an American one. Explain that populism thrives on the perception that the 'system' is rigged. Use a flowchart to link economic displacement—the loss of a sense of agency and status—to the rise of anti-establishment rhetoric. The most important point here is that populists don't just attack trade; they attack the 'Global Elite' who manage it. This allows us to bridge the gap between economic data and social psychology. I suggest using the phrase 'The Geography of Discontent' to describe how urban hubs flourish while rural hinterlands feel abandoned, creating a spatial dimension to modern political polarization.

Now, introduce the 'Democratic Deficit' as the structural villain of the story. Visualize this as a triangle involving the Citizen, the State, and International Organizations (like the WTO or IMF). Explain that as more decisions move to the international level to facilitate smooth trade, the local voter feels their ballot matters less and less. This is the 'Golden Straitjacket'—the idea that no matter who you vote for, the economic policy remains the same because of global commitments. We must emphasize that this perceived loss of sovereignty is the fuel for 'Take Back Control' movements. Avoid the trap of framing populism as purely irrational; instead, show it as a reaction to a real disconnect between global economic management and local democratic accountability.

To apply these concepts, transition to an exercise where students must map specific populist slogans to the 'losers of trade' logic we identified in Lecture 4.1. For instance, if a politician promises to 'bring back coal,' which economic theory explains why that industry left, and why is that promise so potent? This exercise is designed to reveal if students can move past the surface-level rhetoric of news headlines and see the underlying structural tensions. Conclude by suggesting that the 'backlash' isn't just an obstacle to globalization—it might be its defining limit. This sets the stage for our final session on Economic Nationalism, where we see how governments are starting to prioritize 'security' and 'sovereignty' over the very efficiency we’ve studied all unit.

tasks: Connect the 'losers of trade' from Lecture 4.1 to specific populist voting patterns.
Explain the concept of 'democratic deficit' in global economic governance.

sessions.title: Economic Nationalism
sessions.description: This session covers the return of 'geoeconomics'—the use of economic instruments to achieve geopolitical goals, such as sanctions, export controls, and decoupling. You will be able to analyze how states are now prioritizing security over economic efficiency. This serves as the 'bottleneck' synthesis, explaining why the liberal order of the 1990s is currently under immense strain.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start this final synthesis session by visually dismantling the 'Golden Arches Theory of Conflict Prevention'—the 1990s idea that economic integration would make war obsolete. Draw a large scale on the board with 'Economic Efficiency' on one side and 'National Security' on the other. Explain that for decades, the world tipped toward efficiency, but we are now witnessing a violent re-balancing. Introduce 'Geoeconomics' not as a new concept, but as the return of statecraft where the logic of conflict is expressed through the grammar of commerce. This transition is vital because it marks the end of the 'End of History' era and the beginning of a fragmented, competitive international order.

Moving into the mechanics of this shift, define 'Decoupling' and 'De-risking' by using the analogy of a high-voltage power grid. Decoupling is the total severance of wires—a hard break that assumes the other party is an irreconcilable threat. De-risking, the more nuanced and currently favored approach, is like installing surge protectors and diversifying power sources; it is the strategic thinning of dependencies in critical sectors like semiconductors or green energy while maintaining trade in non-sensitive goods. Address a common misconception here: learners often think de-risking is just 'decoupling lite.' Clarify that while decoupling is an outcome, de-risking is a risk-management strategy that accepts some interdependence but tries to eliminate its coercive potential.

Next, focus on 'Weaponized Interdependence.' Visualize a hub-and-spoke network on the whiteboard. Explain how the very networks that made the world efficient—global payment systems like SWIFT, or the monopoly of specific patent holders—are now being used as choke points. This is where you introduce the evaluation of economic sanctions. Rather than listing types of sanctions, lead a discussion on why they often fail to change state behavior but succeed in signaling resolve or degrading long-term capability. The 'bottleneck' to highlight here is the unintended consequence: when states use their economic dominance as a weapon, they incentivize others to build parallel systems, potentially leading to a more fractured and less stable global economy.

Conclude by challenging the learners to synthesize the entire unit through a 'Sanction vs. Strategic Autonomy' exercise. Ask them to imagine a scenario where a major trading partner invades a neighbor. The task is to identify which dependencies (from the GVCs discussed in Session 2) would be the first to be weaponized and what the cost of 'economic nationalism' would be for the domestic consumer. This final beat is designed to reveal the tension between the voter's desire for cheap goods and the state's requirement for security. End the session by positioning this tension as the defining characteristic of the 21st-century global order, setting the stage for the final unit on modern complexities like climate and cyber-warfare.

tasks: Define 'decoupling' and 'de-risking' in the context of modern trade relations.
Evaluate the effectiveness of economic sanctions as a tool of foreign policy.
